about.title: San Bruno Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: San Bruno sees a steady mix of retail centers, multi-unit housing, and office parks along corridors like El Camino Real and near the I-280/I-380 interchange, all places where uneven walkways, wet floors, or poor lighting can lead to a serious fall. Unlike a car crash, a slip and fall case in California hinges on proving the property owner or manager knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn visitors in time. That means what happened in the minutes and hours after your fall matters: photos of the spill or broken step, witness names, and store surveillance footage before it's overwritten or deleted. San Mateo County property owners and their insurers often dispute notice and liability, so having documentation early can make a real difference. LawProactive doesn't practice law, but we can connect you with an attorney who investigates these details and works on a contingency basis, meaning there's no fee unless your case results in a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About Notice and Evidence Early

items.title: Proving the Owner Knew or Should Have Known
items.desc: California premises law requires showing the property owner had actual or constructive notice of the hazard. An attorney can help gather maintenance logs, prior complaints, and inspection records to build that case.

items.title: Surveillance Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many San Bruno businesses overwrite security footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation request out quickly can be the difference between having evidence and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, Your Claim
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're partly responsible for a fall, you can still pursue compensation reduced by your share of fault rather than being barred entirely.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in San Bruno?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit against a private property owner. If a government entity, like the City of San Bruno or a public transit stop, is involved, the deadline is much shorter and requires an earlier claim process. Because these timelines vary, it's worth getting a case reviewed sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if my fall happened at a shopping center along El Camino Real?
items.answer: Shopping centers often involve multiple responsible parties, such as the individual store, the property management company, and sometimes a maintenance contractor. Sorting out who had notice of the hazard and who was responsible for fixing it takes investigation, which is something an attorney in our network can help pursue.

items.question: Do I need to prove the property owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, California law generally requires showing the owner or manager knew, or reasonably should have known, about the dangerous condition and failed to address it. This is often the most contested part of a premises case, which is why documenting the scene and requesting surveillance footage quickly matters.
